chapter_theme: In the Buddha debate Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist account of continuity: she rejects the flame, wind and stream as examples of a series, presses the Buddha on how a deed bears fruit across moments, dismantles his doctrine of the trace (vasana) carried like flower scent into a pot, argues that total perishing would make release automatic, and reduces his balance-beam image of simultaneous arising and perishing to nothing.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha himself, whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam

611.reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's plea that his school too speaks of an unbroken continuity of arisings, called santana, and answers that the wind, the flame and the stream poured from a water-pot will not serve as examples of it, since in each two things are real.
611.nuance: The 'two' of line 4 is taken as a lasting stuff and its passing states (air, oil or water beside the gust, the tongue of fire, the falling stream), so each of the Buddhist's own examples is turned into a case of something that persists; the verse does not spell the two out.

claims.claim: the arisings of a thing form an unbroken continuity (santana), as a flame, the wind or a stream does
the flame, the wind and the stream are not examples of bare succession, since something real persists in each

612.reading: She puts a dilemma: if the continuity is only a notion, it is like the knowing of the mad, the dreamer or the possessed, which does not answer to anything; if it is a real thing, then, Buddha, his words have no meaning.

claims.claim: if the continuity is a real thing, the teaching that nothing lasts loses its meaning

613.reading: She asks the Buddha how, on his account, he can show the stages of ageing, the fine smallness of a thing's beginning, the growth that opens out moment by moment, and its decline.
613.nuance: Ageing and growth by degrees need something that grows and ages; the point is implied by the question rather than stated. The third line (சாத்திரத்தால் அத் தவிரன்கட் டாழ்ச்சியும்) is obscure and its sense is guessed.

claims.claim: ageing, growth and decline by degrees cannot be shown if each moment perishes wholly

614.reading: What use, she asks, is telling of the many aeons and the merit of the unblinking one, if he says the fruit comes in the very moment a thing arises; and if he says it comes down the line afterwards, then the deed goes on and on and exists.
614.nuance: The aeons (கப்பம்) are the Bodhisattva's long striving told in the birth stories; she makes them pointless under momentariness, or else makes the deed a lasting thing.

claims.claim: the fruit of a deed arises in the same moment as the deed
if a deed's fruit comes later down the series, the deed persists until then

615.reading: Even if he calls the earlier moment a cause, she says, it is no cause, since nothing of it goes into the next; mocking him as a god of logic who speaks folly, she asks whether the village tank fills when no water comes down the channel.

claims.claim: a cause must pass something into its effect, as water must flow down the channel to fill a tank

616.reading: What has arisen perishes utterly without staying, and the wholly non-existent cannot arise, she says, so his endless talk of continuity is only words, and she calls him one whose way is to lay many low and feed on them.
616.nuance: The last line is abuse: it charges the Buddhist teaching with deceiving people for a living, not only with error.

claims.claim: what is wholly non-existent cannot come to arise

617.reading: The narrator tells that when the Buddha had argued the continuity of arising by the flame and she had shown each point faulty and pressed him hard, he searched for an answer and set out to establish the doctrine of vasana, the trace that carries over.
617.nuance: The word before வாசனை (சடருடை) is doubtful; the sense that he now turns to the trace is clear from the verses that follow.
617.event: Pressed on the flame example, the Buddha turns to defend continuity by the doctrine of the trace (vasana).

618.reading: Neelakesi states his new claim, that after a moment perishes all its powers cling to what follows as the scent of fragrant flowers is found in a pot, and says that the tenet he holds does not fit these examples.

claims.claim: after a moment perishes its powers pass into the next, as flower scent stays in a pot

619.reading: While the earlier moment exists the later does not yet, and when the later is had the earlier is gone, she argues, so in what way can a trace join the two.

claims.claim: a trace cannot pass between two moments that never exist together

620.reading: If he answers that pot and flower exist together and so the scent can join them without fault, she replies that perishing and birth are never together, which is just why she said the moments do not join.

claims.claim: scent passes because pot and flower are present together
the perishing of one moment and the birth of the next are not simultaneous, so nothing joins them

621.reading: Something that goes whole from within the perishing moment into the arising one cannot be called a mere trace, she says; posited so, it is a firebrand that burns his whole side.
621.nuance: If whatever crosses over crosses entire, it is a lasting thing, which is the Jain's point; the firebrand turns the Buddhist's own device against him.

claims.claim: what passes entire from one moment to the next is a persisting thing, not a trace

622.reading: He speaks of the pollen's smell that came from the blossom into the new pot as passing to the cool water, she says; but if the scent perishes along with the flower, whose would the trace be? She tells him, as one who does not know, to answer with understanding.
622.nuance: The image is the old one of the new pot that perfumes the water put in it. ஓதன in line 3 is unclear; it is read as 'the scent that is spoken of'.

claims.claim: a scent must belong to some bearer; if the flower's scent perished with it, the trace in the water belongs to nothing

623.reading: He keeps saying 'trace, trace' along the line, she says, and assenting to it achieves nothing; let him come and show what thing it is that the pathiri flower, kept in the vessel, smeared with its scent.
623.nuance: பாசனம் is taken as the vessel (Sanskrit bhajana): she demands the lasting receiver that a scent needs.

claims.claim: a scent is received by some thing, and the Buddhist must name what receives the trace

624.reading: If he says the trace, perishing in the flower and arising in the new pot, is found everywhere, she says in mockery, then let him hail it as an auspicious arrival and think on the fine feet of his god.
624.nuance: The second half is hard: சுவாகதம் is taken as 'welcome' and the line as sarcasm that a trace found everywhere would be a lasting, all-pervading thing fit to be worshipped; the word division of தேவன் or ஏவன் is not certain.

claims.claim: the trace perishes in the flower and arises in the pot, and is found everywhere

625.reading: If the trace too perishes utterly, she argues, it must have a trace of its own and the series runs on without end; if he says no such reckoning applies to it, then none applies to the first either, and the faults she named at the start stand.

claims.claim: a trace that itself perishes needs a further trace, without end

626.reading: If he says the scent went over, it did not perish; if he says it did not go, the smell too is absent; and she boasts that when she, knowing the good, declares this right, no one can say before her that it is not.
626.nuance: The second line's ending (இல்லற்க) is odd; the dilemma of the first two lines is clear.

claims.claim: either the scent went over and so did not perish, or it did not go and the smell is not there

627.reading: Since he makes perishing total, she argues, the release he speaks of must be that very perishing, so nirvana would come alike, and briefly, to those who join in great austerity and to those without virtue.
627.nuance: The argument makes Buddhist release a by-product of momentariness, which the Buddhist would deny: the Manimekalai's teacher places release in seeing impermanence and the cessation of craving, not in the perishing of moments. நீடலதே is read as 'not lasting'.

claims.claim: if every moment perishes entirely, release is that perishing and comes alike to the ascetic and the vicious

628.reading: If he declares that, since arising follows down a line, this reply is the excellence of his path, she says she will make plain that it is faulty, and bids him listen with a clear head.
628.nuance: The first two lines are compressed and the exact claim she quotes is uncertain; சவறு is taken as 'fault'.

claims.claim: arising by succession down a line answers the objection and is the strength of the Buddha's path

629.reading: Does a moment bring forth its successor and then perish, she asks, or does the later arising come when it perishes; of the two, which is his way of arising? Let him say it plainly, without darkness.

630.reading: If a moment produces the next and then perishes, she says, there is contact between them, as with a woman who bears a child and dies; if he says the perishing one never meets what follows, let him show a son to a maiden who has died.
630.nuance: A dead virgin has no son: the image makes a cause that never meets its effect as impossible as a child without a mother.

claims.claim: a cause that never meets its effect cannot produce it

631.reading: Both ways fail, she says, perishing after giving birth and perishing as the next arises, so he is made to give up both; she then asks him, as Vaman, whether he ever spoke of perishing so as to make it forgotten.
631.nuance: வாம is read as the vocative of வாமன், a name for the Buddha. The second half is obscure.

632.reading: She tells him not to spin round with many evasions: if he shows the rising and sinking of the two ends of a balance as the arising and perishing of moments, both ends must be there, and if the end that is gone does not exist, the image does not hold.
632.nuance: The balance-beam is the Buddhist's figure for a cause perishing at the same instant as its effect arises; her reply turns on both pans being present together. The third line is read loosely.

claims.claim: the cause's perishing and the effect's arising are simultaneous, like the two ends of a balance beam

633.reading: For what does not exist there is no perishing, she says, just as no one speaks of the size or fineness of a crow's tooth; the narrator adds that she, whose tongue moves only for the good, asked him whether any word could be said of such a thing.

claims.claim: what does not exist cannot perish, as a crow's tooth has no size

634.reading: On his view there is no balance, she concludes: the beam too is absent, the two ends have no way to stand, rising and falling are mixed everywhere, and what is seen at the end is void.
634.nuance: அட்டகம் is taken as the beam or frame of the balance; if it too is momentary, the image collapses. The verse turns the Buddhist figure into emptiness (பாழ்) as a reproach, not a doctrine.

claims.claim: if every part is momentary, the balance and its two ends do not exist and the image ends in nothing

links.note: Earlier the Buddha likened the aggregates, arising and perishing in one moment, to the tip of a lamp's flame; here Neelakesi refuses the flame as an example of continuity because two real things are in it.
links.teaches: The flame the Buddha offered as the very picture of momentary arising is claimed by the Jain for her own side, since a lamp shows a lasting fuel beside its passing tip, so one image serves both doctrines depending on which of its two parts is looked at.

links.note: The Buddha said the deed exists and its fruit exists but there is no doer; Neelakesi answers that if the fruit comes later down the line, the deed itself must last until then.
links.teaches: Granting deed and fruit while denying a doer moves the lasting thing from the agent to the deed: the Jain shows that the Buddha's karma needs a persistence somewhere, and the debate is over where to put it.

links.note: The pathiri scent left in a new pot appears in the Kundalakesi debate, where Neelakesi used it to argue a soul outlasts the body, and here as the Buddha's own example of the trace.
links.teaches: The same pot of scent is read two ways in one epic: against Kundalakesi Neelakesi took the lingering scent as proof that something outlasts its source, and against the Buddha she denies it can show a trace passing between moments that never coexist.

links.note: Against Mokkalan she said the scent in the sherd belongs to the flower, whose particles stay there and carry it; here she grants pot and flower coexist but denies that successive moments do.
links.teaches: Her earlier answer explains why the pot example cannot help the Buddha: the scent passes only because flower-matter is physically present with the pot, and no such co-presence exists between a perished moment and the next.

links.note: Against Kundalakesi she argued that if nothing of the first moment is in the next, knowing fails, and if something is, it is a soul; here she shows the two moments never exist together for a trace to pass.
links.teaches: The dilemma put to Kundalakesi about what a trace carries is sharpened into a point about time: before asking what the trace holds, the Jain asks when it could cross, and finds no instant shared by the two moments.

links.note: The Naladiyar's new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers, an image of the unlearned gaining sense from the learned; Neelakesi attacks the same image as the Buddha's proof of a trace that outlives the flower.
links.teaches: The ethical image of borrowed fragrance only works if the scent has a lasting bearer, the flower-dust in the pot, so the Jain debater's demand to know whose the scent is shows what the Naladiyar's figure quietly assumes about company and influence.

gains.a: the debate verse is seen to be contesting a well-worn Tamil figure, not a stray example, which explains why the Buddhist chose it and why the Jain must dismantle it
gains.b: the quatrain's simile of good company is shown to rest on a theory of how a quality passes, which the epic makes an open question between schools

links.note: Mokkalan argued that on the Jain view an ascetic's soul would not exist in the time to come and keeping the precepts would be wasted toil; here Neelakesi argues that on the Buddha's view nirvana comes alike to the ascetic and the vicious.
links.teaches: Each side charges the other's metaphysics with making austerity pointless, which shows that in these debates a doctrine of time and persistence was tested by whether it could still reward discipline.

links.note: The Buddha said continuity arising from a seed by potency is change, and that release is not other than this; Neelakesi replies that if each moment perishes entirely, release is that perishing and needs no austerity.
links.teaches: The Buddha's own phrase that release is not other than the change of the series is what lets the Jain equate nirvana with every moment's end, so the Buddha's wording supplies the premise of her reductio.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher makes release the seeing that the links are sorrow, unstable and without self; the Neelakesi's Jain argues that momentariness would make release the mere perishing of each moment.
links.teaches: Set beside the Buddhist epic's own account, the Jain charge is seen to aim at a version of Buddhism the Buddhist teacher would not own, since there release is an insight gained by those who see impermanence, not the impermanence itself.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher says there is no arising for a hare's horn, the mode of denial resting on what is not; Neelakesi says there is no perishing for what does not exist, as there is no size to a crow's tooth.
links.teaches: Both schools grant the same rule for the non-existent, and the Jain uses it against the Buddhist: if a perished moment is as unreal as a hare's horn, it cannot also be the thing whose perishing gives rise to the next.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008, since vaadham is taken for alchemy

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: புத்தா (613), புத்த (612); id as declared in neelakesi ch010

new_concepts.gloss: the continuity or series (santana): in Buddhist teaching the unbroken succession of momentary arisings that stands in for a lasting self or thing
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: சந்தானம் (611, 612); தொடர்ச்சி (611, 616, 617)

new_concepts.gloss: the trace or perfuming (vasana): the Buddhist account of how a perished moment's powers pass into the next, as scent passes from flower to pot
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: வாசனை (617, 619, 621 to 625)

new_concepts.gloss: the moment (ksana): the least span of time, in Buddhist teaching the whole life of each thing that arises and perishes
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: கணந்தோறு (613), அக்கணத்து (614)

source_issues: 629 line 3: the edition's '•' is the old encoding of ஃ (repaired in the core).
617 line 4: சடருடை before வாசனை is doubtful, perhaps corrupt.
626 line 2: இல்லற்க is an odd form; the sense of the line is doubtful.
628 line 3: யேலுந் before சவறது looks miswritten (expected யேனும் or யேலும்).
624 lines 3-4: the word division of சுவாகதம் போந்ததென் றேவன் றிருந்தடி is uncertain.
Most verses have no speech verb; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the story, from என்றாள் (618, 628, 629, 624) and from the vocatives to the Buddha (612, 613, 631).
